title: AVL trees
content:
# AVL trees * The binary-search-tree section explained that repeated insertions and deletions can make a tree degenerate into a linked list. All operations then degrade from $O(\log n)$ to $O(n)$ time. In the example below, just two deletions turn the binary search tree into a linked list. ![An AVL-tree example degenerating after deletions](avl_tree.assets/avltree_degradation_from_removing_node.svg) Likewise, inserting two nodes into the perfect binary tree below makes it heavily skewed to the left, degrading lookup performance. ![An AVL-tree example degenerating after insertions](avl_tree.assets/avltree_degradation_from_inserting_node.svg) In 1962, G. M. Adelson-Velsky and E. M. Landis introduced the AVL tree in their paper “An algorithm for the organization of information.” They described operations that prevent degeneration through repeated insertions and deletions, keeping the time complexity of operations at $O(\log n)$. AVL trees therefore maintain efficient data operations when insertions, deletions, lookups, and updates are frequent, making them valuable in practice. ## AVL tree terminology An AVL tree is both a binary search tree and a balanced binary tree, satisfying the properties of both. It is therefore a balanced binary search tree. ### Node height AVL operations need node heights, so add a `height` variable to the node class: ```snippet avl_tree_node ``` A node's height is the distance to its farthest leaf, measured in edges. A leaf has height $0$, while a missing node has height $-1$. We create two helper functions to retrieve and update a node's height: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{update_height} ``` ### Balance factor A node's balance factor is its left subtree's height minus its right subtree's height. A missing node has balance factor $0$. Wrap this calculation in a function for convenient use: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{balance_factor} ``` !!! tip If a node's balance factor is $f$, every node in an AVL tree satisfies $-1 \le f \le 1$. ## AVL tree rotations The defining operation of an AVL tree is rotation, which restores balance without changing the inorder traversal sequence. **A rotation preserves the binary-search-tree property while restoring the balanced-tree property**. A node whose balance factor has absolute value $> 1$ is “unbalanced.” Depending on the imbalance, we use one of four rotations: right, left, right-then-left, or left-then-right. Let us examine them in detail. ### Right rotation In the figure below, balance factors appear beneath the nodes. Viewed from the bottom up, node 3 is the first unbalanced node. Focus on the subtree rooted there, naming its root `node` and its left child `child`. A right rotation restores balance while preserving the binary-search-tree property. === "<1>" ![Steps of a right rotation](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_rotate_step1.svg) === "<2>" ![avltree_right_rotate_step2](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_rotate_step2.svg) === "<3>" ![avltree_right_rotate_step3](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_rotate_step3.svg) === "<4>" ![avltree_right_rotate_step4](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_rotate_step4.svg) If `child` has a right child, denoted by `grand_child`, add one step to the rotation: make `grand_child` the left child of `node`, as shown below. ![A right rotation with grand_child](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_rotate_with_grandchild.svg) “Rotating right” is a visual description; the implementation updates node pointers: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{right_rotate} ``` ### Left rotation For the mirror image of the unbalanced tree above, perform a left rotation, as shown below. ![A left rotation](avl_tree.assets/avltree_left_rotate.svg) Similarly, if `child` has a left child, denoted by `grand_child`, make it the right child of `node` during the rotation. ![A left rotation with grand_child](avl_tree.assets/avltree_left_rotate_with_grandchild.svg) **Right and left rotations are mirror images, as are the imbalances they resolve**. To obtain left-rotation code, exchange every `left` and `right` in the right-rotation implementation: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{left_rotate} ``` ### Left-then-right rotation For unbalanced node 3 below, neither a left nor a right rotation alone restores balance. First rotate `child` to the left, then rotate `node` to the right. ![A left-then-right rotation](avl_tree.assets/avltree_left_right_rotate.svg) ### Right-then-left rotation For the mirror-image case below, first rotate `child` to the right, then rotate `node` to the left. ![A right-then-left rotation](avl_tree.assets/avltree_right_left_rotate.svg) ### Choosing a rotation The four cases below correspond to the examples above and require, respectively, right, left-then-right, right-then-left, and left rotations. ![The four AVL rotation cases](avl_tree.assets/avltree_rotation_cases.svg) As the table below shows, the signs of the unbalanced node's balance factor and that of the child on its taller side determine the case.

Table   Conditions for choosing a rotation

| Unbalanced node's balance factor | Child's balance factor | Rotation | | ------------------ | ---------------- | ---------------- | | $> 1$ (left-heavy) | $\geq 0$ | Right | | $> 1$ (left-heavy) | $<0$ | Left, then right | | $< -1$ (right-heavy) | $\leq 0$ | Left | | $< -1$ (right-heavy) | $>0$ | Right, then left | Wrap the rotation logic in one function. **It can then handle every imbalance and restore the affected node's balance**. The code is as follows: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{rotate} ``` ## Common AVL tree operations ### Inserting a node Insertion largely follows the binary-search-tree procedure. The difference is that inserting a node may unbalance nodes along the path to the root. **Starting at the inserted node, work upward and perform rotations to restore balance at every affected node**: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{insert_helper} ``` ### Deleting a node Similarly, extend binary-search-tree deletion with rotations from the bottom up to restore balance at every affected node: ```src [file]{avl_tree}-[class]{avl_tree}-[func]{remove_helper} ``` ### Finding a node Lookup is identical to binary-search-tree lookup, so we will not repeat it here. ## Typical applications - Organizing and storing large datasets, particularly when lookups are frequent and insertions and deletions are less frequent. - Building database indexing systems. - Red-black trees are another common kind of balanced binary search tree. Their balance requirements are looser than those of AVL trees, so insertion and deletion need fewer rotations and are more efficient on average.
